title: Trust thyself
hook: every heart vibrates to that iron string: trust thyself (Self-Reliance)

segments.voice: Yesterday, banned from Harvard: a hard talk, a sincere uproar, and Emerson declining to argue back. Your line was true and kind. Did the true thing get said, and gently? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

A meeting. Someone across the table makes a point, and everybody nods. It's good. It's exactly right. And at the end of the table, someone else goes quiet, because the same thought crossed their mind earlier, and they let it go. It seemed too obvious, or too odd, or not quite their place to say. Now it belongs to somebody else. Emerson starts his essay Self-Reliance very near that moment, and he builds a whole philosophy out of it. A little further on come two words, set down like a bell rung once: trust thyself.
screen: `SOMEONE SAYS THE THOUGHT.` → `ANOTHER HAD IT FIRST.` → `TWO WORDS: TRUST THYSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the rejected thought. Near the start of Self-Reliance, Emerson writes: "In every work of genius we recognize our own rejected thoughts: they come back to us with a certain alienated majesty." Alienated majesty. Your own idea, coming back grand and strange, wearing someone else's name. He says we dismiss our own thoughts simply because they're ours. Second, the gleam. Emerson says a person should learn to watch for the gleam of light that flashes across the mind from within, more than the brilliance of all the poets and sages. Not instead of them. More than them. The books matter. But the flash is yours, and only you can catch it. Third, the iron string. Then come the famous words: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string." It's an instrument picture. A string pulled tight, and when it's struck, every heart hums with it. Emerson is saying the call to self-trust isn't strange or rare. Everyone, he says, already feels it. Fourth, what it does not mean. Despite the title, the essay isn't mainly about money, or never asking for help. And trust here isn't stubbornness, or doing whatever you feel like. It's quieter than that. It's giving your own honest perception a fair hearing before you hand it over to the crowd. The quiet thought at the end of that table may have been wrong. But Emerson's point is that nobody found out, because it wasn't trusted long enough to be said.
screen: `OUR OWN REJECTED THOUGHTS.` · `WATCH THE GLEAM FROM WITHIN.` · `EVERY HEART VIBRATES.` · `NOT STUBBORNNESS: A FAIR HEARING.` · then, large: `TRUST THYSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one instinct. Settle, and breathe out slowly. Let your mind go quiet enough to notice what comes up on its own. Somewhere in there is a small, steady knowing you've been talking yourself out of. Something to start. Something to stop. Someone to call. You don't have to act on it yet. Just let it be heard, all the way through, without the usual voice that says, who are you to think that? Give the instinct a fair hearing. The bell holds the time.
Trust thyself. Emerson's two words from Self-Reliance: give your own honest perception a fair hearing, because every heart, he says, vibrates to that iron string. Today's word.
Your line: trust thyself. Today, when a thought flashes up and you start to wave it off, say it out loud instead, once, and see what happens. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of Self-Reliance take 'trust thyself' as a call to give their own honest perception a fair hearing, alongside books and other people's opinions rather than beneath them.

notes: Confirm exact wording and punctuation of both quotations against the 1841 text.

The 'gleam of light' passage is paraphrased: a man should learn to detect and watch that gleam of light which flashes across his mind from within, more than the lustre of the firmament of bards and sages.
'Everyone, he says, already feels it' reads 'every heart vibrates' as Emerson's claim; it is attributed to him, not stated by the narrator.
The meeting hook is an illustration, not a source claim.
Editor: softened 'isn't about money' to 'isn't mainly about money' (the essay does discuss property and charity); 'readers often' to 'some readers'.
